trial_name: ALBIOS — Albumin Replacement in Severe Sepsis/Septic Shock (2014)
citation: Caironi P, Tognoni G, Masson S, Fumagalli R, Pesenti A, Romero M, et al. Albumin replacement in patients with severe sepsis or septic shock. N Engl J Med. 2014;370(15):1412-1421.
one_liner: In adults with severe sepsis/septic shock, protocolised 20% albumin replacement to maintain serum albumin ≥30 g/L did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with crystalloids alone.

pico.population: Adults (≥18 years) admitted to ICU with severe sepsis (Sepsis-1 era) within the prior 24 hours, including patients with septic shock.
pico.intervention: 20% albumin plus crystalloids, with albumin dosing guided by daily serum albumin to target ≥30 g/L for up to 28 days or ICU discharge.
pico.comparison: Crystalloids alone for volume replacement, using the same haemodynamic targets; albumin and other colloids were discouraged.

background.existing_knowledge: Colloids (including human albumin) were widely used in sepsis for presumed intravascular volume expansion, yet clinically important outcome benefit over crystalloids remained uncertain. The SAFE trial (ICU-wide) found no overall mortality difference between albumin and saline; its pre-specified severe sepsis subgroup suggested possible benefit, but this was hypothesis-generating.
background.knowledge_gap: Observational and mechanistic work suggested potential non-oncotic effects of albumin (endothelial/glycocalyx interactions, binding/transport, antioxidant capacity), but translation to patient-centred benefit was unproven.
background.hypothesis: In adults with severe sepsis (including septic shock), adding 20% albumin (with a protocolised target serum albumin ≥30 g/L) to crystalloids reduces 28-day mortality compared with crystalloids alone.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, open-label, controlled trial in 100 ICUs (Italy); central computer-generated allocation; stratified by ICU and by time from severe sepsis criteria to randomisation (<6 hours vs 6–24 hours).

inclusion: Adults (≥18 years) admitted to ICU with severe sepsis (Sepsis-1 era) within the prior 24 hours, including patients with septic shock.
exclusion: Clinical conditions mandating albumin, contraindication/allergy, and other protocol-specified exclusions (e.g., consent constraints).

methods.intervention: 20% albumin plus crystalloids, with albumin dosing guided by daily serum albumin to target ≥30 g/L for up to 28 days or ICU discharge (whichever occurred first), alongside haemodynamic resuscitation using standard targets.
methods.comparison: Crystalloids alone for volume replacement, using the same haemodynamic targets; albumin and other colloids were discouraged except under defined exceptions/violations.
methods.sample_size_power: 1350 patients planned to detect a 17% relative reduction in 28-day mortality (from 45% to 37.4%) with 80% power at 5% significance; interim assessment allowed sample-size re-estimation up to ~1800.
secondary_outcomes: Time to suspension of vasopressor/inotropic agents

headline_bullets: No difference in 28-day mortality: 31.8% albumin vs 32.0% crystalloids (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.87–1.14, P=0.94).
No overall 90-day mortality benefit: 41.1% vs 43.6% (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.85–1.05, P=0.29).
A septic shock subgroup signal at 90 days (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.77–0.99) was attenuated with covariate adjustment (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77–1.01, P=0.07).
Albumin achieved biochemical separation and modest haemodynamic effects without improving global organ dysfunction.

outcomes_table.outcome: Time to suspension of vasopressor/inotropic agents (days; median)
outcomes_table.note: Tertiary outcome; susceptible to practice variation in an open-label design.
Direction towards more RRT with albumin.

outcomes_table.outcome: Serum albumin at day 1 (g/L; mean ± SD)
Mean arterial pressure at 6 hours (mmHg; mean ± SD)
Net fluid balance at day 2 (mL; median [IQR])
outcomes_table.note: Daily net balance differences were statistically significant on selected days; total 7-day net balance did not differ (P=0.13).

outcomes_table.outcome: Total administered fluids over 7 days (mL; median)
Packed red blood cell volumes (mL; median [IQR])

subgroup_table.note: Attenuated with covariate adjustment (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77–1.01, P=0.07).

subgroup_table.subgroup: No septic shock at enrolment (90-day mortality)
subgroup_table.note: Directionally opposite to septic shock subgroup.

safety: No statistically significant difference in renal-replacement therapy (24.6% vs 21.4%, P=0.11).
No difference in acute kidney injury incidence (21.9% vs 22.7%, P=0.71).

domains.notes: Central, computer-generated assignment sequence; stratified by ICU and enrolment time stratum; allocation concealment was likely adequate up to assignment.

Open-label design risks co-intervention differences (e.g., fluid choices, transfusion thresholds, vasopressor weaning practices); mortality is objective, but tertiary outcomes (vasopressor duration) are more vulnerable to bias.
1818 randomised; outcome denominators indicate limited missing follow-up for mortality (e.g., 28-day mortality assessed in 895/903 vs 900/907).

Protocol violations were common: 377/903 (41.8%) in the albumin arm were noncompliant with albumin administration at least once; 336/907 (37.1%) in the crystalloid arm received albumin at least once; synthetic colloids were administered as violations in 205/903 (22.7%) vs 214/907 (23.6%).
Broadly similar at baseline for key reported variables (e.g., median age 70 vs 69 years; female sex 39.9% vs 39.4%; SAPS II median 48 vs 48).

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate: allocation procedures were robust and endpoints objective, but open-label conduct with substantial protocol deviations/crossover and potential co-intervention imbalances likely diluted any true treatment effect and complicate interpretation of tertiary outcomes.

domains.notes: Broad adult ICU severe sepsis cohort (median age ~70 years) across 100 ICUs supports generalisability within high-income ICU systems; however, definitions and care bundles reflect the Sepsis-1/EGDT era, not Sepsis-3 or contemporary resuscitation paradigms.

The tested strategy requires serial albumin measurement and access to 20% albumin; practice environments with limited albumin supply or cost constraints may not adopt a 'target ≥30 g/L' approach. Findings apply to sustained albumin replacement (hyperoncotic 20%) in addition to crystalloids, rather than a simple substitution of crystalloids with iso-oncotic albumin as an initial resuscitation bolus.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is reasonable for similar ICUs with access to albumin and serial labs, but translation to contemporary sepsis definitions and to resource-limited settings is constrained by changing standard care and the intervention’s resource intensity.

strengths: Pragmatic severe sepsis population including septic shock.
Demonstrated biochemical and physiological separation with detailed supplemental reporting.
limitations: High protocol nonadherence and clinically meaningful contamination (albumin exposure in control).
Power assumptions not met due to lower-than-expected baseline mortality.
Subgroup findings vulnerable to multiplicity and residual confounding in adjusted analyses.

critical_appraisal.summary: A large, well-randomised trial with an objective primary outcome, but open-label conduct, high crossover, and lower-than-expected event rate reduce confidence in the null finding and limit interpretation of secondary endpoints.
strengths: Central, stratified randomisation with allocation concealment.
Objective primary outcome (mortality) with minimal loss to follow-up.
Clear biochemical separation confirming protocol delivery.
weaknesses: Open-label design introduces risk of performance and detection bias for secondary/tertiary outcomes.
High protocol nonadherence and crossover (37.1% of controls received albumin) likely biased results toward the null.
Lower-than-anticipated baseline mortality reduced statistical power for the primary endpoint.

sections.authors_conclusion: In patients with severe sepsis, albumin replacement in addition to crystalloids did not improve survival compared with crystalloids alone.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Routine protocolised albumin replacement to target a serum albumin ≥30 g/L does not improve survival in severe sepsis/septic shock and should not be standard practice.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients with severe sepsis/septic shock in settings with access to albumin and serial lab monitoring.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Albumin is harmful or has no role as a rescue fluid in patients requiring large volumes of crystalloids; the trial tested a sustained replacement strategy, not a single resuscitation bolus.
implementation_caveats: The intervention is resource-intensive (requires serial albumin measurement and 20% albumin).
A hypothesis-generating signal in the septic shock subgroup does not justify routine use without confirmation.

controversies.notes: The intervention was a sustained 'albumin replacement to target' strategy rather than albumin as the primary initial resuscitation fluid; extrapolation to early resuscitation fluid choice is limited.
The high rate of deviations (including albumin exposure in 37.1% of controls) risks underestimating any true effect and complicates causal interpretation of secondary/tertiary outcomes.

The apparent 90-day benefit in septic shock was accompanied by opposite direction in non-shock and was attenuated in covariate-adjusted analyses; this creates a credible 'multiplicity + residual confounding' explanation for a borderline P=0.03 interaction finding.
Lower-than-anticipated mortality reduced the ability to detect modest absolute benefits, particularly when contamination and practice heterogeneity are present.

Post-ALBIOS systematic reviews/meta-analyses have been mixed, often suggesting no clear all-cause mortality benefit overall, while some report possible benefit signals in septic shock or specific albumin concentrations; conclusions are sensitive to inclusion criteria.

Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines recommend crystalloids as first-line and suggest considering albumin when substantial amounts of crystalloids are required (weak/conditional recommendation, low certainty), whereas newer albumin-specific guidance generally discourages routine albumin use in many critical care indications.

context_related_trials.relation: Preceding ICU-wide trial comparing albumin vs saline; found no overall mortality difference. Its pre-specified severe sepsis subgroup suggested possible benefit, providing part of the rationale for ALBIOS.

unresolved_questions: Does albumin as a primary resuscitation fluid (rather than a sustained replacement strategy) confer a mortality benefit in septic shock?
Is there a true, reproducible mortality benefit in the septic shock subgroup, or is the ALBIOS signal a product of multiplicity and confounding?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Protocolised albumin replacement to a target serum albumin ≥30 g/L does not improve survival in severe sepsis and should not be routine practice.
